On hearing this, Taizong nodded and sighed, “So it has indeed come to pass. I once asked the Ten Kings of the Underworld, ‘Are the old and young of my household safe?’ They answered, ‘All are safe, but we fear that Your Majesty’s imperial sister will be short-lived.’ Their words have proved true.” Everyone in the palace came grieving bitterly. When they reached the shade of the flowers to look, they saw that the princess was still breathing faintly. The Tang emperor said, “Do not weep! Do not weep! You may frighten her.” He stepped forward, raised her head with his imperial hands, and called, “Imperial sister, awake! Awake!” The princess suddenly turned over and cried, “Husband, do not go so fast! Wait for me!” Taizong said, “Imperial sister, it is we who are here.” The princess raised her head, opened her eyes, and looked about. “Who are you,” she demanded, “that you dare pull at me?” Taizong said, “We are your imperial brother and sister-in-law.” The princess said, “What imperial brother and sister-in-law could I possibly have? My maiden name is Li, and my childhood name is Li Cuilian. My husband’s surname is Liu and his given name is Quan. We are both natives of Junzhou. Three months ago, I removed my golden hairpin at the front gate to give alms to a monk. My husband reproached me for leaving the inner quarters without permission and failing in a wife’s propriety, and scolded me a few times. Anger choked my breast, so I hung myself from a beam with a white silk sash, leaving behind a son and daughter who wept day and night. p.src: As the Tang emperor sat in court, an officer in attendance suddenly reported, “Your Majesty, Liu Quan, the man who delivered the melons and fruit, has returned to life and awaits your command outside the court gate.” The Tang emperor was greatly astonished and hastily ordered Liu Quan summoned. Liu Quan entered and prostrated himself on the vermilion steps. Taizong asked, “How did the delivery of the melons and fruit go?” Liu Quan replied, “Your servant carried the melons and fruit on his head and went straight to the Gate of Ghosts. From there I was led to the Hall of the Underworld, where I met the Ten Kings, presented the fruit, and fully conveyed Your Majesty’s cordial gratitude. The Kings were delighted and asked me to convey their many respects to Your Majesty, saying, ‘Emperor Taizong is truly a sovereign of honor and virtue!’” The Tang emperor asked, “What did you see in the underworld?” Liu Quan replied, “Your servant did not travel far and saw nothing much. I only heard the King of the Underworld ask about my native place and name. I told him the whole story: how I had abandoned my home and children and volunteered to deliver the melons because my wife had hanged herself. He immediately sent a ghostly messenger to bring my wife, and we met below the Hall of the Underworld. Meanwhile, they examined the register of life and death and said that my wife and I were both destined to live long enough to attain immortality, so they sent ghostly messengers to escort us back. Your servant walked ahead and my wife followed behind, and happily I returned to life. But I do not know where my wife’s soul has entered.” The Tang emperor asked in astonishment, “Did the King of the Underworld say anything about your wife?” Liu Quan replied, “The King himself said nothing at first. I only heard a ghostly messenger say, ‘Li Cuilian has been dead for a long time, and her corpse no longer exists.’ Then the King of the Underworld said, ‘Li Yuying, the Tang emperor’s imperial sister, is now due an early death. Let Cuilian borrow Yuying’s corpse and return to life at once.’ Your servant does not know what place ‘the Tang emperor’s imperial sister’ might mean or where her home is, so I have not yet been able to search for her.”

p.src: Now it happened that Yuchi Gong took the treasury of gold and silver to Kaifeng Prefecture in Henan and made inquiries. Xiang Liang, it turned out, earned his living by selling water, while he and his wife, Madam Zhang, also sold black-glazed basins and earthenware outside their door. Whatever little money they made sufficed only for their daily expenses; yet, however much or little remained, they gave alms and meals to monks, bought paper ingots of gold and silver, entered them against a treasury account, and burned them as offerings. Through these good deeds, such blessings had come to them. In the world of the living he was a poor man devoted to good works, but in the other world he was a wealthy elder with jade amassed and gold piled high. When Yuchi Gong delivered the gold and silver to their door, Master and Mistress Xiang were so terrified that their souls nearly fled their bodies. Officials of the prefecture had come as well, and horses and carriages crowded outside the thatched cottage. The old couple, struck witless and dumb, knelt on the ground and did nothing but kowtow in obeisance. Yuchi Gong said, “Good people, please rise. Though I am an imperial envoy, I have brought my sovereign’s gold and silver to repay you.” Trembling, Xiang Liang replied, “This humble man has never lent anyone gold or silver. How could I dare accept wealth of unknown origin?” Yuchi Gong said, “I have learned that you are indeed a poor man. Yet you feed monks and give alms, spending all you can spare on paper ingots of gold and silver, which you burn and register with the netherworld. Thus you have amassed money in the underworld. Our Emperor Taizong died for three days and then returned to life. While in the underworld, he borrowed a treasury of gold and silver from you, and now its full amount has been brought to repay you. Accept it all, so that I may return and report that the imperial command has been fulfilled.” Xiang Liang and his wife merely bowed in worship toward Heaven and dared not accept it. They said, “If we accepted all this gold and silver, we would soon be dead. Though we burned paper offerings and registered them to a treasury, those are hidden matters of the unseen world. Moreover, what proof is there that His Majesty borrowed gold and silver in that world? We most certainly dare not accept it.” Yuchi Gong said, “His Majesty said that Judge Cui stood surety for the things he borrowed from you and can bear witness to it. Please accept it.” Xiang Liang said, “Even if it costs me my life, I dare not accept it.”

p.src: Seeing that he persisted in refusing, Yuchi Gong had no choice but to write a memorial and send a man to present it to the throne. When Taizong read the memorial and learned that Xiang Liang would not accept the gold and silver, he said, “He is truly a good and virtuous elder.” He at once decreed that Hu Jingde should use the gold and silver to restore a monastery for him, erect shrines to the living couple, and invite monks to perform good works; this would count as repayment all the same. When the decree arrived, Jingde faced the imperial palace, thanked the emperor for his grace, and proclaimed the command so that all might know it. The gold and silver were then used to purchase an unencumbered plot within the city, fifty mu in extent. Construction began there, and a monastery named “The Imperially Founded Xiangguo Monastery” was erected. To its left stood shrines to Master and Mistress Xiang while they yet lived. A stone monument was carved with the words “Construction Supervised by Yuchi Gong.” This is the present-day Great Xiangguo Monastery.

p.src: When Taizong heard these words, he cast the memorial before his assembled ministers for deliberation. At that time the chancellor Xiao Yu stepped from the ranks, bowed his head, and memorialized: “The Buddha’s teaching has flourished through many dynasties. It promotes good and restrains evil, and lends unseen aid to the state. There is no reason to cast it aside. The Buddha is a sage. Whoever denies a sage has no law in him; I beg that he be severely punished.” Fu Yi disputed with Xiao Yu, saying, “The rites are founded upon serving one’s parents and one’s sovereign. Yet the Buddhist abandons his parents to leave the household, sets himself as a commoner against the Son of Heaven, and, in claiming to perpetuate ritual, acts contrary to those nearest to him. Xiao Yu was not born from a hollow mulberry tree, yet he follows a fatherless doctrine. He is precisely what is meant by saying that the unfilial recognize no parent.” Xiao Yu merely joined his palms and said, “Hell was established precisely for men such as this.” Taizong summoned Zhang Daoyuan, Minister of the Imperial Stud, and Zhang Shiheng, Director of the Secretariat, and asked what response might follow from performing Buddhist rites to cultivate blessings. The two ministers replied, “The Buddha’s teaching rests in purity, benevolence, and forbearance; its fruit is true enlightenment and emptiness. Emperor Wu of Northern Zhou assigned the three teachings their respective ranks. Chan Master Dahui composed verses of profound and far-reaching import, and wherever he received offerings, miraculous signs never failed to appear. The Fifth Patriarch was reincarnated, and Bodhidharma manifested his form. From ancient times all have said that the Three Teachings are supremely venerable and may neither be reviled nor abolished. We humbly beg Your Majesty to examine this wisely and render an enlightened judgment.” Taizong was greatly pleased and said, “Your words accord with reason. If anyone raises the matter again, he shall be punished.” He then ordered Wei Zheng, Xiao Yu, and Zhang Daoyuan to invite the Buddhist clergy and select one man of great virtue to serve as master of the altar and establish the ritual sanctuary. They all touched their heads to the floor, thanked the emperor for his grace, and withdrew. From that time a law was enacted: whoever reviled monks or slandered the Buddha was to have an arm severed.

p.src: Upon the platform the Master recited for a while the Scripture on Receiving Birth and Delivering the Dead, discoursed for a while on the Heavenly Precious Register for Securing the Realm, and then proclaimed for a while the Scroll Exhorting the Cultivation of Merit. The Bodhisattva stepped forward, struck the precious platform, and cried in a stern, loud voice, “You monk! You know only how to expound the Lesser Vehicle. Can you expound the Great Vehicle?” Hearing this, Xuanzang was overjoyed. He wheeled around, leaped down from the platform, and saluted the Bodhisattva with joined hands, saying, “Venerable teacher, forgive your disciple for failing to recognize and honor you. All the monks here before us have spoken only of the doctrines of the Lesser Vehicle; I do not know what the doctrines of the Great Vehicle are like.” The Bodhisattva said, “These doctrines of the Lesser Vehicle cannot deliver the dead and raise them to a higher realm; they can only help one blend with the common world and conceal one’s radiance. I possess the three collections of the Great Vehicle Dharma, which can raise the dead to heaven, deliver those in distress from suffering, cultivate a body of immeasurable longevity, and attain the state of neither coming nor going.”

p.src: While this exchange was taking place, the official overseeing incense and patrolling the hall hurriedly reported to the Tang emperor, “Just as the Master was expounding the wondrous Dharma, two scabby wandering monks dragged him down and began babbling nonsense.” The emperor ordered that they be seized and brought before him. A great many people shoved the two monks into the rear Dharma hall. When they saw Taizong, the monks neither raised their hands in salute nor bowed, but looked up and said, “What does Your Majesty wish to ask us?” The Tang emperor recognized him and said, “Are you the monk who presented the cassock the other day?” The Bodhisattva replied, “I am.” Taizong said, “Since you came here to hear the sermon, you should simply have eaten some vegetarian fare and left. Why did you argue recklessly with my Master, disturb the scripture hall, and disrupt my Buddhist service?” The Bodhisattva said, “Your Master expounds the doctrines of the Lesser Vehicle, which cannot deliver the dead and raise them to heaven. I possess the three collections of the Great Vehicle Dharma, which can deliver the dead from suffering and grant an imperishable body of long life.” Taizong’s face grew solemn as he asked with delight, “Where are those scriptures of the Great Vehicle?” The Bodhisattva said, “They are with our Buddha, the Tathagata, at the Great Thunderclap Monastery in the land of India, in the Great Western Heaven. They can untie the knots of a hundred grievances and dispel undeserved calamities.” Taizong asked, “Do you remember them?” The Bodhisattva replied, “I do.” Taizong was overjoyed and said, “Have the Master conduct them to the platform and invite them to preach.”

p.src: After reading the verse, Taizong immediately commanded the monks, “For now, bring this splendid assembly to a close. When I have sent someone to obtain the Great Vehicle scriptures, we shall once again offer our sincere devotion and renew this virtuous work to its blessed completion.” All the officials obeyed. Then, in the monastery, the emperor asked, “Who is willing to bear my command, journey to the Western Heaven, worship the Buddha, and seek the scriptures?” Before he had even finished asking, the Master stepped out from beside him, saluted before the throne, and said, “Though this poor monk is of little ability, I am willing to serve Your Majesty with the devotion of a dog or horse. I shall seek the true scriptures for you and pray that Your Majesty’s realm remain forever secure.” The Tang emperor was overjoyed. He stepped forward, raised Xuanzang with his own imperial hands, and said, “If you truly can fulfill this loyal and worthy undertaking, fearing neither the length of the journey nor the hardship of crossing mountains and rivers, I shall gladly swear brotherhood with you.” Xuanzang bowed his head to the floor and thanked him for the imperial favor. The Tang emperor was indeed a man of surpassing virtue. Before the Buddha in the monastery, he exchanged four bows with Xuanzang and addressed him as “my imperial younger brother, the holy monk.” Xuanzang, unable to express the fullness of his gratitude, said, “Your Majesty, what virtue or ability does this poor monk possess, that I should dare receive such gracious favor from Heaven? Once I depart, I shall spare neither life nor strength until I reach the Western Heaven. If I fail to reach the Western Heaven and obtain the true scriptures, then even in death I shall not dare return to this country, but shall fall forever into the hell of perdition.” He then offered incense before the Buddha and swore this oath. The Tang emperor was greatly pleased. He ordered the imperial carriage to return, intending to choose an auspicious day, issue the travel documents, and send Xuanzang on his way. Thus the emperor returned to the palace, and all dispersed.

p.src: Xuanzang likewise returned to Hongfu Monastery. The many monks of the monastery and several of his disciples had already heard about the quest for the scriptures. They all came to see him and asked, “Is it true that you have vowed to journey to the Western Heaven?” Xuanzang said, “It is true.” His disciples said, “Master, we have often heard it said that the road to the Western Heaven is long and beset by even more tigers, leopards, demons, and monsters. We fear that you may go and never return, unable even to preserve your life.” Xuanzang said, “I have already made a mighty and solemn vow: if I fail to obtain the true scriptures, may I fall forever into the hell of perdition. Above all, I have received the sovereign’s favor and must devote myself loyally to repaying my country. My journey will indeed lead into a boundless unknown, and whether fortune or calamity awaits cannot be told.” He added, “My disciples, after I leave, whether two or three years pass, or five or seven, watch the pine branches inside the monastery gate. If their tips turn eastward, I shall soon return; otherwise, I shall never return.” All the disciples engraved these words firmly upon their hearts.

p.src: Early the next morning, Emperor Taizong held court and assembled his civil and military officials. He had the passport for the scripture quest drawn up and stamped with the imperial seal authorizing free passage. An official of the Imperial Observatory memorialized, “Today the auspicious star that honors mankind is ascendant; it is a fitting day to set out upon a distant journey.” The Tang emperor was delighted. Then a palace attendant announced, “Your Majesty’s brother, the reverend master, awaits your command outside the court gate.” He was immediately summoned into the imperial hall, where the emperor said, “Imperial brother, today is an auspicious day for departure. Here is your passport for crossing the frontiers. I also have a purple-gold alms bowl for you to use when seeking food along the way. I have also chosen two attendants accustomed to long journeys. And I bestow upon you a horse to carry you on your distant journey. You may now set forth.” Xuanzang was overjoyed. He at once gave thanks for the imperial favor, accepted the gifts, and had no thought of delaying any longer. The Tang emperor ordered out his carriage and, together with many officials, escorted him beyond the pass. There they found the monks of Hongfu Monastery and all his disciples waiting beyond the pass with Xuanzang’s clothing for winter and summer. When the Tang emperor saw them, he first ordered the baggage and horse made ready, then commanded an official to take up the flagon and pour wine. Taizong raised the cup and asked, “By what honored religious name are you known, imperial brother?” Xuanzang replied, “This poor monk is a man who has left the household life and has not presumed to assume any such title.” Taizong said, “The Bodhisattva told us that in the Western Heaven there is a collection of scriptures called the Tripitaka. Why not take your name from the scriptures you seek and call yourself Tripitaka?” Xuanzang again gave thanks for the imperial favor. Taking the wine offered by the emperor, he said, “Your Majesty, wine stands foremost among the prohibitions of the monastic order. Since becoming a monk, this poor monk has never learned to drink it.” Taizong said, “Your departure today is unlike any ordinary occasion. This is unfermented wine. Drink this single cup, that I may fully express my wish to speed you on your way.” Tripitaka dared not refuse. He accepted the wine and was just about to drink when Taizong lowered his head, scooped up a pinch of earth with his imperial fingers, and flicked it into the cup. Tripitaka did not understand his meaning. Taizong smiled and said, “Imperial brother, once you depart for the Western Heaven, when will you return?” Tripitaka replied, “Within three years I shall return directly to our exalted realm.” Taizong said, “The years will be long, the mountains distant, and the roads far. Drink this wine, imperial brother: better to cherish a pinch of earth from one’s homeland than to covet ten thousand taels of gold in a foreign land.” Only then did Tripitaka understand the meaning of the pinch of earth. He thanked the emperor once more, drained the cup, took his leave, and passed beyond the frontier. The Tang emperor returned in his carriage.
